Failed results are still committed and lost (no retry/DLQ)

Offset completion happens in a `finally` block, so `complete_offset()` runs even when `result_processor` raises, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` already swallows all exceptions internally. Combined with the offset tracker, a message whose processing permanently fails is still considered done, committed, and never retried or routed to a DLQ — it is silently lost, contradicting the class docstring's 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Similarly, submit() (line 317) catches exceptions from decoding/grouping and marks the offset complete, dropping those messages. Errors must leave the offset outstanding (or send to DLQ) rather than be committed.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items instead of draining

OrderedQueueWorker.run() tests `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `queue.get()`. In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 231) every worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True, and only afterwards is `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` called. Because the loop exits as soon as the flag is set, a worker processes at most the one item it had already fetched and then drops everything still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain semantics never take effect. In-flight results are silently discarded on a graceful shutdown. The loop should keep calling `get()` and break only when it raises `queue.ShutDown`.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each work queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never blocks; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` only records a gauge. If a group's single worker falls behind (e.g. one slow subscription), its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps polling and advancing/committing offsets, consuming memory and risking OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is therefore false. Use a bounded queue (maxsize) and either block in submit() or stop polling when queues are full.

arroyo Commit invoked from a background thread

The commit function passed into create_with_partitions (arroyo's `Commit`) is called every second from a dedicated `commit_thread`, i.e. concurrently with the consumer's poll loop and rebalance handling, whereas every other mode commits from the strategy's processing thread. arroyo's Commit is not designed for cross-thread invocation; if it is not fully thread-safe this can corrupt or lose committed offsets. Either serialize commit calls onto the strategy thread (a lock coordinated with poll/join) or confirm arroyo's Commit is safe to call from another thread.

join() ignores its timeout and can block for ~100s

join(timeout) discards the argument and delegates to close(), which calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() joins each worker sequentially with a hard-coded `timeout=5.0`; with the default 20 queues that is up to ~100 seconds of blocking in the worst case, far beyond arroyo's expected join timeout and potentially past the broker's max.poll.interval.ms during shutdown/rebalance. Respect the passed timeout and join workers against a shared deadline.

test_stats_reporting is racy against active workers

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a pool with 3 already-running worker threads and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. The workers can consume all items before get_stats() executes, making total_items 0 and flaking the test. Make it deterministic by asserting on a state that cannot race with consumption (e.g. pause/block the workers, or check committed counts rather than instantaneous queue depth).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

The denial key concatenates user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with literal "_" separators. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores and resource name/folder are caller-controlled, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. A denial cached for one resource would then deny an unrelated resource. Use length-prefixed or escaped components, or hash a structured key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer checks collide

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, subject UID, action, resource name, and folder, but not the identity type. Anonymous and renderer subjects both resolve to user UID "0" (for example anonymous:0 and render:0), and users and service accounts can also share a UID. A denial written for one principal is therefore returned for another principal on the same action/resource/folder. Concretely, an anonymous Check for dashboards:read/dash1 stores key org-12.perm_0_dashboards:read_dash1_, and a later renderer Check for the same dashboard hits that key and is denied without consulting renderer permissions, breaking rendering. Include the identity type (or full subject type) in the denial key.

Every distinct denied resource name causes a fresh permission DB query

When cached identity permissions exist but do not allow the requested resource, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and queries the permission store. The denial cache only remembers the exact (action, name, parent) tuple, so callers can send checks for arbitrary distinct dashboard/folder UIDs (for example anonymous probes of /api/dashboards/uid/<random>) and force one permission DB query per UID. Previously these cache-hit checks were served without touching the DB. This is a DB-load/DoS regression; consider coalescing or marking a user/action as freshly queried rather than falling back per resource name.

Tests seed the denial cache manually and never verify Check populates it

The new denial-cache test manually calls permDenialCache.Set before invoking Check. There is no test that performs a Check returning false from the permission store and then asserts the denial is written, nor a test that a denial for one identity type does not affect another identity type. As a result, a regression where Check never writes denials, writes them under a mismatched key, or collides anonymous and renderer entries would pass the current test suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana list items rendered without a React key

In the `rules.map` switch in `FilterViewResults`, the `'grafana'` branch now returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without a `key` prop. Every other branch (`'datasource'`, default) still passes `key={key}`. The loop already computes a stable `key` (getRuleKey) and the old `GrafanaRuleLoader` was passed `key={key}`, so this is a regression. A `map` that returns elements without keys triggers React 'Each child in a list should have a unique key' warnings and forces reconciliation by array index, which can cause stale state/misrendering when the list grows or reorders. Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element.

false_negatives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action is never shown for Grafana rules in the ruler-less list view

The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (`handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier)`). In the new list view (`RuleActionsButtons.V2`, used by `GrafanaRuleListItem`), only `promRule` is passed and `rulerRule` is always `undefined`, so the Delete item never renders even though `canDelete` is now correctly computed from the prom-rule abilities. This means users can no longer delete Grafana-managed rules from the alert list (the GrafanaGroupLoader test that grants `AlertingRuleDelete` and asserts only 4 menu items confirms it). `RuleActionsButtons.V2` already ignores the arguments and calls `showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`, so the `rulerRule` requirement in this gate (and the `handleDelete` signature) should be relaxed to use the identifier for the list-view path if delete is meant to remain available.

Federated rule-group detection silently removed from useAllAlertRuleAbilities

The refactored (deprecated) `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifierV2)`. The old implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRule's group; the new shared `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` (with a TODO) because it only receives a rule and a group identifier, not the group's `source_tenants`. As a result, federated Mimir/Metrics-Enterprise rule groups (which must be treated as immutable) are no longer marked immutable in any caller of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`, so the UI will offer Edit/Delete/Pause for rules that the backend considers read-only. This is a behavioral regression for existing consumers that still use this hook.

View link no longer carries returnTo for Grafana rules

The `href` for the rule is built as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view')`, dropping the `returnTo` query parameter that the previous `GrafanaRuleLoader`/`GrafanaRuleListItem` added via `createReturnTo()` (`createRelativeUrl(path, { returnTo })`). Consequently, navigating from the rule list/group view into a rule's detail page loses the origin, so the detail page's back navigation no longer returns the user to the filtered/hierarchical list. If the returnTo behavior is still desired, the `returnTo` parameter should be restored.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range splitting guard is untested after interpolation

Interpolation now runs before the `partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` split. `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep queries that use `$__range` out of splitting, precisely because `$__range` is supposed to be resolved from each query's time range. There is no test covering a `$__range` query after interpolation. If the datasource's `applyTemplateVariables` resolves `$__range`/`$__range_ms`/`$__range_s` from `request.scopedVars`, `isQueryWithRangeVariable` will no longer find the variable, the guard silently stops protecting the query, and it gets time-sliced with `$__range` computed per sub-range rather than for the full range. Add a test asserting a `$__range` query still lands in the non-splitting partition after interpolation.

Shard path now interpolates every target twice

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates each target with `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` here, then passes those already-interpolated targets as sub-requests into `runSplitQuery` (line 163). Since this PR, `runSplitQuery` also interpolates its targets (querySplitting.ts:299), so in the sharding path every target goes through `applyTemplateVariables`/`templateSrv.replace` twice. The updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' asserts `applyTemplateVariables` was called 5 times for a single query (1 here + 1 per each of the 4 shard sub-requests), which confirms the duplication; before this PR the shard path interpolated exactly once. A second replace pass over already-resolved text is usually a no-op, but it corrupts expressions whose interpolated values themselves contain `$name`/`${name}` sequences (e.g. a label value or regex containing `$`) and it doubles templating work. Guard against this, e.g. add an option so `runSplitQuery` skips interpolation when the caller already did it, or stop pre-interpolating in the shard path and expose the selector needed for `fetchLabelValues` another way.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards context, making the new FromContext-based logging path untestable

TestLogger.FromContext ignores its context.Context argument and returns a brand-new empty TestLogger. The refactored LoggerMiddleware now obtains contextual attributes exclusively via FromContext, so any test using this fake can never observe whether the attributes were actually propagated. The fake silently masks exactly the behavior this PR introduces. It should copy/record the contextual attributes from the context (or the log call should include them) so tests can assert the merged output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Refactor moves pluginId/endpoint/uname/ds labels from explicit log params to FromContext with no test

Before this PR the "Plugin Request Completed" log line explicitly added pluginId, endpoint, uname (dsName/dsUID) and traceID from the request's PluginContext. Those explicit params were deleted; the line now depends entirely on the contextual attributes added by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware being read back through m.logger.FromContext(ctx). If the middleware ordering, the WithContextualAttributes plumbing, or the grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext type-assertion ever fails, these labels silently disappear from the log line and nothing detects it. No test covers this path (the renamed metrics test only checks Prometheus metrics), so this behavior change is unverified. At minimum a test should wrap the logger middleware with a logger that records FromContext output and assert pluginId/endpoint/labels are present.

Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename

The file and symbol were renamed from Instrumentation to Metrics, but the test function is still `func TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This leaves the rename inconsistent and makes the test hard to locate by name; it should be renamed to TestMetricsMiddleware.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert check is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices (line 110) and then, if under the limit, performs a separate INSERT/ON CONFLICT (line 149) in a different DB session with no transaction or lock between them. Under concurrent anonymous requests two or more new devices can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, pushing the table past the configured limit. The limit is therefore only approximately enforced under load. Consider counting and inserting in one transaction/locking, or enforcing the cap in SQL.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Returning the raw limit error from Authenticate fails anonymous requests instead of denying gracefully

When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns `nil, err`. Because this is the anonymous authn client, a returned error aborts authentication for the whole request rather than yielding a successful anonymous identity, so a device that is over the limit gets an authentication failure (generic error/401-500) on the requests where the DB path runs. Combined with the localCache being primed before the DB call, this produces intermittent failures: the first request fails and later ones (cache hit) succeed. There is no user-facing handling for 'device limit reached'; the decision to hard-fail the request (vs. logging and continuing, or mapping to a controlled response) should be made explicit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device is cached before DB write, so a rejected device is let through on retry

tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache (line 87) and only afterwards calls anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is now propagated (line 147) and by client.go aborts authentication. However the cache entry is never removed on this failure. Any subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early `localCache.Get` return (line 83) and succeeds without touching the DB. The net effect is that the device limit only blocks the first request of a device (per instance) and then silently allows it, the device is never recorded in the DB/count, and because the cache is per-process the behavior also differs across HA instances. The cache must be populated only after a successful DB write (or deleted on error).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Limit test only covers rejection of a new device; no coverage that existing devices still update

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit verifies only that a brand-new device is rejected when the limit is reached. It does not assert the complementary and important behavior that an already-registered, active device continues to update successfully at the limit (the updateDevice path returning rowsAffected > 0), nor does it cover the localCache-before-DB-write interaction that lets a rejected device through on retry. Without these cases the bypass and the 'existing devices keep working' contract are untested.

anonymousDeviceLimit typed as number | undefined but backend always sends a number

FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit is an int64 without omitempty, so the API always serializes a number (0 when unset / unlimited). The TS type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the GrafanaBootConfig default `undefined` therefore misrepresent the wire contract: consumers checking for `undefined` to mean 'unset' will never see it, they always get 0. The type should be `number` (with 0 documented as unlimited) to match the backend.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with full ID lists

The new batch code logs normal, successful cleanup work with `r.log.Error` and includes the entire `ids` slice and generated `cond`. This occurs in `CleanAnnotations` (by age and count) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On a table with many matching rows a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs, every cleanup cycle, even when `err` is nil. This floods error logs/alerting and can slow the cleanup job itself. Use Debug/Trace and log counts or errors, not full ID lists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The cleanup loop ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, query history, etc.) runs ten times as often. `clean` is synchronous and can take up to the 9-minute timeout; because ticker events are buffered as one pending tick, a long-running cleanup can be followed immediately by another, effectively running cleanup continuously and increasing database load/contention. Unless a tenfold increase in global cleanup frequency is intended and coordinated, this change should be reverted.

false_positives.candidate:
New SQLite batch-size test does not actually exceed SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER

The new test case creates 40,003 annotations, but cleanup is run per annotation type and each type has only about 13,334 rows. Therefore no DELETE statement ever contains more than about 13,334 IDs, which is below SQLite >=3.32's 32,766 parameter limit. The test would still pass if the large-batch/inlining fallback were removed, so it does not verify the boundary it claims to cover. It needs more than 32,766 annotations of a single type (or an equivalent setup producing a single batch above the limit).

SQLite large-batch ID list is built in quadratic time

In the SQLite fallback, the ID list is materialized with repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. This makes construction O(n^2) in the number of IDs; a batch in the tens of thousands can copy gigabytes and create GC pressure during cleanup. Use `strings.Builder`, a byte slice, or `strings.Join` to build the list in linear time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 records several operations under the wrong metric or label

The metrics in this file are mis-attributed. A unified-storage create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 45), and a unified-storage update failure is also recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 129), even though no legacy call has happened. Delete success passes the object `name` as the `kind` argument to `recordStorageDuration` (line 106), which both mislabels the series and creates unbounded `kind` label cardinality. DeleteCollection's async legacy call records `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration` (line 166). These produce incorrect dashboards/alerts and misleading legacy vs. storage latency/error rates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

Mode 3 launches the legacy write in a goroutine using the incoming request context: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. In Go's HTTP server, the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, and these methods return the unified-storage result immediately after starting the goroutine. The legacy `Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` calls (also at lines 110, 135 and 163) therefore commonly run with an already-canceled context, so the shadow write to legacy fails and the safety copy is never made. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving request values) or a fresh context with an explicit timeout.

Create error test configures the wrong store and will hit an unexpected mock call

The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets `setupLegacyFn` to return an error and never sets a `Storage.Create` expectation. Mode 3's `Create` calls `Storage.Create` first, so this test invokes the storage mock without an expectation and fails with a testify panic rather than exercising a unified-storage failure. Configure `setupStorageFn` for the error and, if the legacy path is to be covered, set the legacy expectation separately.

Delete/DeleteCollection success tests do not account for the async legacy mock call

The success cases for `TestMode3_Delete` and `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` only set up the Storage mock. Mode 3 always launches a goroutine that calls `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection`, but there is no legacy expectation and the tests do not wait for the goroutine. With testify's bare `mock.Mock`, the unexpected call panics; even if it did not, the test returns before the legacy write happens and never asserts that the shadow delete occurred. Add legacy expectations and a synchronization mechanism (or refactor to inject a synchronous executor) to verify the async write.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order

All mode 3 legacy writes are independent goroutines with no per-object serialization. Two sequential updates to the same object can complete their legacy writes in reverse order, leaving legacy with the older state; a delete followed by a re-create can likewise leave the shadow store missing or containing an object after the unified store already reflects the opposite operation. Because the legacy write is meant as a safety copy, this silently makes the two stores diverge. A per-key queue/worker or version/order check is needed if legacy is expected to remain consistent.

Legacy write failures in async mode are never logged

Every async goroutine discards the legacy error and only calls a metrics recording function, e.g. `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. There is no `log.Error`, unlike the previous synchronous implementation. Since these writes are fire-and-forget, operators have no log evidence when the shadow write fails, making the safety mechanism effectively undiagnosable. Log the error (including object identity and method) in each async legacy path.

Mode 3 integration subtests read legacy before the async shadow write can complete

The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which assumes writes made through the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy `/api/playlists` API (for example the list comparison around lines 516-531 and `getFromBothAPIs` after k8s create/update/delete). Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so the legacy read can race ahead of the shadow write and see stale or missing data. These mode 3 subtests will be flaky/failing even if the implementation is correct; they need to poll/wait for legacy convergence or use a synchronous test mode for immediate-visibility assertions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

After the fast-path read finds `entryPointAssetsCache == nil` and the goroutine acquires `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`, the cache is never checked again. With two concurrent requests in a non-dev environment, both can observe nil, then serialize on the lock and each call `readWebAssetsFromFile`. The second goroutine performs redundant I/O and, worse, overwrites the cache populated by the first goroutine; if its own read fails, it clobbers a valid cache with nil and reports an error. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` while holding the write lock and return the cached value if it has been populated by another goroutine.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for concurrent GetWebAssets calls

This PR specifically fixes a data race, but no test exercises concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`. Without a test that starts multiple goroutines against an uninitialized cache and runs under `-race`, a future regression could reintroduce the race or the missing double-check behavior without being detected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false and ignores the feature flag

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled` from `FlagSqlExpressions`, then returns `false` in both branches. As a result the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle has no effect: SQL expressions are permanently disabled even when the flag is enabled. If permanent disable is intended, the flag lookup is dead code and should be removed; if the flag is supposed to control availability, this is a logic error that makes the toggle ineffective and prevents safely re-enabling the feature through the existing flag.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command path is disabled only via the stub DB, not an explicit gate

`NewSQLCommand` (used by `UnmarshalSQLCommand` for the legacy query path) has no explicit SQL-disabled check. It currently fails only because the new `pkg/expr/sql.DB` methods return `not implemented`, which makes `sql.TablesList` error out. If the DB implementation is later restored or replaced, this path will execute SQL without consulting `FlagSqlExpressions` or the new `ExpressionQueryReader` guard, re-enabling the vulnerable feature. The disable should be enforced at command creation or execution rather than relying on the stub error.

No regression test for disabled SQL expressions

The security gate for `QueryTypeSQL` was added without any test. There is no regression test asserting that a SQL expression query is rejected even when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled, nor that non-SQL expression types still parse. Without such a test, a later change to the guard or the stub DB could silently restore the RCE/LFI-capable SQL expression path.

User-facing error incorrectly says SQL expressions are not implemented

When a SQL expression is submitted, the new error is `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The feature was implemented and is being intentionally disabled for security, so this message misrepresents the state and can lead users to believe their Grafana build lacks the feature rather than that SQL expressions are blocked. Return a clear disabled/unsupported message instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can race and overwrite each other

Removing the lock around the whole BuildIndex function leaves no per-key serialization: getOrCreateIndex does GetIndex and then BuildIndex without any lock, and BuildIndex does not re-check the cache before building. Two concurrent searches/watch events for the same NamespacedResource can therefore build two indexes. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt the index; for in-memory indexes the second build overwrites the first in the cache, so a search/watch that already got the first index keeps writing to an index the cache will never return again. Add a per-key singleflight/build lock and re-check the cache under that lock before starting a build.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the index cache without holding cacheMu

BuildIndex now mutates b.cache under cacheMu, but TotalDocs ranges over the same map without any lock. If TotalDocs is called while an index build stores its result, this is a Go map concurrent read/write race and can panic. Take cacheMu.RLock while iterating.

false_positives.candidate:
Index build goroutines race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed

Inside init, every errgroup goroutine assigns to the shared outer err variable and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. One goroutine can overwrite the error from another before it returns, so group.Wait may report success even when an index build failed; the count used for the span/event is also racy. Use a local err in each goroutine and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

Postgres integration test is skipped instead of fixing startup init failure

The PR adds a skip for postgres to the storage-server integration test, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. This PR changes unified storage initialization to happen synchronously during server construction, so disabling the postgres case hides a possible regression in the new startup behavior and leaves the storage-server target without postgres integration coverage. Fix the underlying failure or add equivalent coverage before merging.

Stop no longer prevents requests because handlers no longer observe initErr

Stop sets s.initErr to a stopping/stopped error, and the per-RPC s.Init(ctx) calls used to return that error so requests arriving after shutdown failed fast. Those calls were removed without adding an equivalent stopped-state check, so Create/Update/Delete/List/Watch/Search/etc. can still execute after Stop and after lifecycle.Stop has begun closing or canceling the backend. Add an explicit stopped flag/check in the handlers or in an interceptor.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New IDP cleanup uses wrong alias and leaks all created providers

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") instead of the actual aliases it creates ("idp-alias-" + i, and "idp-alias-20" at line 425). Consequently none of the 21 IDPs created by this test are removed, and cleanup also attempts to delete a provider named "alias" that does not exist. The leaked IDPs can change exact-count assertions in later tests in this class and make reruns order-dependent. Register cleanup with the real alias for each created provider.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Create/remove invalidation for login IDPs is not tested

The new test only creates an IDP with hideOnLogin=true and removes a disabled IDP, i.e. both operations are for non-login IDPs, and asserts that the login caches remain. It never verifies that creating a login-eligible IDP or removing one actually invalidates the getForLogin caches. The create() and remove() invalidation branches added in this PR could be removed or broken and this test would still pass. Add cases that create an enabled/login-visible IDP and remove one, asserting that all login cache entries are cleared.

Login-cache invalidation uses organization-aware original model

update() obtains the original IDP through getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...). For an IDP linked to a disabled organization (or when the organization provider is unavailable), that wrapper's isEnabled() is false even though the raw persisted IDP is enabled and was therefore cached in the login list. If such an IDP is subsequently updated from enabled=true to enabled=false, registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate sees both the wrapped original and the raw updated model as non-login IDPs and returns without invalidating the login caches. The cached getForLogin result then continues to contain an IDP that is no longer login-eligible until another invalidation happens. The invalidation predicate should be evaluated against the raw stored model, not the organization-aware wrapper.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle

getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented/contractually expected to return a BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the Provider of `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType())` (typically the JDK SUN provider, or whatever the default keystore type resolves to). Any consumer that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BouncyCastle algorithm registration/lookup will get the wrong provider and may fail with NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider or silently use different crypto. All other unsupported methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException; this one should do the same unless it genuinely provides a BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded

Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances (write(rBigInteger) and write(sBigInteger)) and throw the results away; the returned value is produced separately by the chained writeDerSeq(...) call. These two statements have no effect and only allocate objects. They are leftover code and should be removed, since they can mislead a reader into thinking the sequence is built from them.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common, and order() is added as an abstract method rather than a default method. Every existing implementation (including third-party providers and the keycloak-client code the PR description says will be synced later) must now add this method; old implementations that do not will fail to compile / fail at link time. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve compatibility while still letting providers opt into precedence.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA round-trip test uses one default-curve key and never verifies the signature

The test generates a single `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, normally P-256) and reuses it for ES256/384/512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is idempotent; it never verifies the produced signature with the public key and never exercises the actual 521-bit curve. Because the padding to `signLength` is symmetric, a wrong per-curve length/endianness/truncation would still round-trip and the test would pass. Generating a key per algorithm's curve and asserting Signature.verify would actually validate curve-specific behavior.

Multi-provider selection is nondeterministic and removes fail-fast FIPS guard

This change removes the previous guard that threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found, and instead silently picks the highest-order provider. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the only provider that is actually disambiguated is AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). If two of the real providers land on the classpath together (e.g. a FIPS deployment that also has the default provider), selection among the equal-order providers falls back to the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is not guaranteed stable across filesystems/containers. The result is that a non-FIPS provider can be chosen silently in a deployment that previously failed fast at startup, disabling FIPS without any error. FIPS should have a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers (or the removed guard should be retained for genuinely conflicting providers).

New provider-ordering selection logic is not covered by tests

detectProvider now sorts multiple providers by order() and ignores the lower-ordered ones, but there is no test that loads multiple CryptoProviders and asserts the highest-order one is selected (or that ties behave sanely). Given this ordering is the central mechanism of the PR, a test using a custom ServiceLoader/classloader with two known-order providers would guard the selection logic against regressions and would have surfaced the equal-order ambiguity noted for the real providers.

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resource lookup uses the wrong owner

The per-client permission lookup passes `server.getId()` as the resource owner, but `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` creates these resources with `resourceServer.getClientId()`. A resource server id and its clientId are different values, so this lookup normally misses. Per-client grants are then ignored (or only the all-clients fallback is evaluated), which breaks permissions such as `MANAGE` or `VIEW` granted for a single client.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resources cannot be found by type

`getClientsWithPermission` queries resources with type `Clients`, but `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` creates individual client resources with `resourceStore.create(...)` and never calls `setType(CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`. Those resources therefore have no type and are not returned here. An admin with only a per-client grant will not get that client in the filtered client list. The all-clients resource is also added to the returned set under its name `Clients`, which is not a client id.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing Clients all-resource can cause a null dereference

When no per-client resource exists, `getResourceTypeResource` can return null if the all-clients `Clients` resource is missing (for example an existing realm that has not been migrated to the new schema). The result is then passed to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)`, which can throw instead of denying access. The code should guard against a null fallback and return false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client resource names are not resolved

`getResourceName` only special-cases the `Users` resource type. For `Clients` it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, but resources created by `getOrCreateResource` have no display name, and the all-clients resource is named `Clients`. Permission/resource listings for client permissions will therefore show null or unhelpful names instead of the client id or a meaningful "All clients" label.

Client role-mapping checks ignore legacy manage-clients and MANAGE grants

`canMapRoles`, `canMapCompositeRoles`, and `canMapClientScopeRoles` only check explicit `MAP_ROLES*` scopes and never call `super` or `canManage(client)`. Under V2, a caller who has the legacy `MANAGE_CLIENTS` role (which `canManage(ClientModel)` still honors) or a `MANAGE` grant on the client will be denied client role mapping, unlike V1 and the other client operations. These methods should include the same manage fallback unless V2 intentionally removes that behavior.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not migrated to the Clients schema

`init` returns immediately when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient()` is already non-null. Realms that initialized the admin-permissions client before this change will never receive the new `Clients` resource type, the `Clients` all-resource, or the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). Creating a Clients permission on such a realm fails in `getScope` (scope does not exist) or hits a missing all-clients resource during evaluation. The schema change needs an upgrade/migration path for existing clients.

Listener can call unsupported V2 cleanup methods

The cleanup listener is gated only by `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1). If V2 is also enabled, `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`, and the client-removal branch calls `clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`. `ClientPermissionsV2` overrides that method to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, so deleting a client can fail with a 500 when both features are enabled. The listener must also account for V2, or the V2 implementation must provide a no-op for this cleanup path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Caution overstates when rolling-updates feature is required

The caution says the Operator will fail unless `rolling-updates` is enabled. The updated UpgradeTest only adds the feature to the CR for explicit `spec.update.strategy` values; for the default (`strategy == null`) it returns before enabling the feature and still expects successful rolling/recreate behavior in `testImageChange[null]` and `testCacheMaxCount[null]`. Either the requirement only applies when `spec.update` is set and the caution should say so, or those tests are missing the required feature and are not exercising the documented gate.

Documented exit codes 3 and 4 are not asserted

The new documented contract has exit code 4 for feature-disabled and changes recreate from 4 to 3. `testFeatureNotEnabled` only checks the error text, and `testWrongVersions` only checks the incompatibility message; neither asserts the exit code. A regression that prints the right text but returns the wrong code would go unnoticed, despite the exit code being the scriptable contract described in `update-compatibility.adoc`.

testMissingOptionOnSave can pass when feature gate exits early

The test only asserts that `Missing required argument` is absent. With the new feature check in `UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()`, a run where `--features=rolling-updates` is not recognized exits with the feature-disabled error before option validation, and this assertion still passes. The test should assert that the metadata command actually ran, for example no feature-disabled error, exit code 0, or metadata output, otherwise it no longer verifies that `--file` is optional.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants group management with only VIEW scope

The global canManage() returns true when the caller has only VIEW on all groups because it evaluates hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE). GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage() before creating a top-level group, so a caller with view-only all-groups permission can create groups. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE; canManage() should require only MANAGE as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group member permission lookup uses authz resource IDs instead of group IDs

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission the callback calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...), but hasPermission treats its first argument as a group id and looks it up with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). For a per-group resource the resource name is the group id, not the resource id, so the lookup falls back to the all-groups resource (or fails), and the method adds groupResource.getId() (an authz resource id) to the granted set. UsersResource then puts those ids into UserModel.GROUPS, so per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are ignored and an all-groups grant can make user search return no users. Use groupResource.getName() (the group id) or evaluate the resource directly, and add the group id, not the resource id.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing realms never receive the new Groups scopes/resources

Adding Groups to SCHEMA is not applied to realms that already have an admin-permissions client. init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null, so existing V2 realms keep only the old Users/Clients scopes and all-resource resources. Group scopes such as view-members and the all-groups resource will be missing; creating group permissions then fails in getOrCreateResource with 'No scopes found' (or getScope throws), and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission can evaluate a null all-groups resource. This needs an upgrade/migration path or an ensure-missing-scopes/resources update.

Group removal cleanup is not registered for V2

Group-removal cleanup is still gated on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and not ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. In a V2-only deployment the listener is never registered, so deleting a group leaves its Groups resource and policies orphaned. If both features are enabled, management(...).groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, causing group deletion to fail. The new Groups resource type needs a V2-safe cleanup path.

Groups resource type is not resolved to a group name for display

getResourceName handles only USERS. For a policy with resourceType Groups it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), and because group resources are named with the group id, the admin console/events show the raw id instead of the group name (and there is no 'All groups' label). Add a GROUPS branch analogous to the USERS branch.

Per-group resources are created without a resource type

getOrCreateResource creates a resource for a group and updates its scopes, but never calls resource.setType(resourceType). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission enumerates group grants with resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...), so per-group resources created here are invisible to that lookup (only the type-tagged 'Groups' all-resource is returned). As a result group-scoped member permissions cannot be found for user search/listing. Set the resource type when creating the resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian account message replaced with Italian text

The new `totpStep1` value is `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian account users will see Italian instructions after this change. The text needs to be restored to a Lithuanian translation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese bundle contains Traditional Chinese text

The new `totpStep1` text `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` uses Traditional Chinese characters and Taiwan-style wording (`手機`, `應用程式`) in the `zh_CN` Simplified Chinese bundle. Users of the Simplified Chinese locale will see mixed script. It should be converted to Simplified Chinese.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Account UI message now uses Java single-brace placeholders

The other account UI error messages in this file use double-brace interpolation such as `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, and `{{2}}`. This change replaces them with single-brace Java-style placeholders and adds a Java `ChoiceFormat` expression (`{2,choice,...}`). The account UI message layer will not substitute those placeholders, so users will see literal `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and the choice text instead of the attribute name and value count. Keep the JS interpolation syntax or format the plural in the UI.

Admin UI message now uses Java single-brace placeholders

This JS admin UI bundle uses double-brace placeholders (`{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, `{{2}}`) throughout. The changed `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value uses single braces and a Java `ChoiceFormat` expression (`{2,choice,...}`), which the admin UI interpolation does not process. The result is a user-visible error message with literal placeholders rather than the attribute name and count.

Lithuanian login message replaced with Italian text

The new `loginTotpStep1` value is `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. This makes the Lithuanian login page show Italian instructions. It should be a Lithuanian translation.

Sanitizer tests cover only rejection cases, not valid HTML The added tests only verify that illegal HTML, unchanged anchor mismatches, and duplicate keys produce errors. There is no test proving that a translation containing HTML allowed by the English source (for example `

`, `
`, ``, or an exact matching anchor) passes without a false positive. This is important because the verifier is now applied to large resource bundles and false positives block the build.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor checks grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

The constructor calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") a second time instead of validating rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId is therefore accepted, and encodeTokenId() would concatenate it as the literal text "null" into the token ID. The error message for the repeated grantType check is also misleading. This should use rawTokenId in the second requireNonNull call.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId checks the wrong substring and has an inverted comparison

The matcher reads items[0].substring(3, 5) for the grant-type shortcut, but the grant shortcut occupies characters 4-5 (0-based indexes 4 and 5) in the 6-character prefix. It also returns false when the substring equals the expected shortcut, which is the inverse of the intended assertion. As a result, the matcher accepts token IDs whose grant shortcut is not the expected one and the updated expectCodeToToken()/expectRefresh()/device/CIBA assertions do not actually validate the encoded grant type. It can also throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException if the prefix is shorter than 5 characters.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Decoder assumes exactly two-character grant shortcuts

getTokenContextFromTokenId() requires encodedContext.length() == 6 and then splits the prefix as 2 chars for session type, 2 for token type, and 2 for grant type. However OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() is documented as usually a 3-letter shortcut and does not enforce a 2-character length. A custom grant factory returning a valid 3-character shortcut (for example "abc") will generate an ID such as "onrtabc:<uuid>", which this decoder rejects with IllegalArgumentException. Any endpoint that later parses token context from such an access token will fail. Either enforce exactly two characters when collecting shortcuts in the factory or make the encoding/decoding format length-independent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

Adding a non-default abstract getShortcut() method to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface is a source and binary compatibility break. Existing custom grant-type factories compiled against the previous interface will not implement this method and can fail at startup with AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() calls gtf.getShortcut() for every registered grant factory. Provide a default implementation or otherwise handle legacy factories without breaking startup.

Removal of public Context copy constructor breaks extension callers

The public OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context context) copy constructor was removed from the Context class. This is a source and binary compatibility break for any custom grant implementation that used it to clone/modify a context. The new grantType field could simply be copied in that constructor, so removing the constructor is unnecessary for the feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exhausted recovery-code credential from user storage is not actually removed

The authenticator now resolves the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which returns the federated (user-storage) credential first when before it only looked at Keycloak's local store. When allCodesUsed() is true the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). That call only deletes from the local credential store; it does not remove or disable a credential owned by a user-storage provider. In addition, models built from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (the shape the user-storage path produces) do not carry the original stored id, so getId() can be null and passing null into the credential store (JPA EntityManager.find) throws IllegalArgumentException. Consequence: for a user-storage user who exhausts all recovery codes the cleanup either throws or is silently ignored, the old federated credential stays in the user store, and it must be relied on that the subsequent required action overwrites it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw recovery codes are persisted to user storage while only hashed codes go local

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list and passes that JSON as the value of the UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). If the user-storage provider persists the value it is handed (as the provided test provider does), the recovery codes are stored in cleartext in external storage. The local branch instead uses credentialModel, which contains only the hashed codes and per-code used flags (see RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.createFromValues). Recovery codes are single-use password-equivalent secrets, so storing them unhashed in an external user store is a meaningful exposure if that store leaks, and the asymmetry means the same credential has different representations depending on where it landed. The code should pass a hashed representation (or otherwise guarantee/require the provider hashes before persisting).

Recovery-codes credential cannot be disabled/removed in the user-storage test provider

The provider now creates, validates and reports recovery-authn-codes as configured, but getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() still only adds CredentialModel.OTP and disableCredentialType() only handles OTP (it logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type: ...' for anything else). Consequently once a recovery-codes credential is written into this user storage it cannot be disabled through the admin or account credential APIs, and that removal path is never tested, so a broken/compromised/exhausted credential cannot be cleaned up.

User-storage recovery codes are replayable and single-use behavior is never exercised

updateCredential stores the raw codes JSON, isValid compares input.getChallengeResponse() against that raw list without ever marking a code used, and getCredentials rebuilds the model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(), which re-hashes the raw codes and sets every code's used flag back to false. As a result allCodesUsed() is always false, getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() always returns code #1, and a recovery code can be used repeatedly for a user in this provider. The new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin does only one login with the first code, so it does not cover the single-use guarantee or the 'all codes used -> re-configure' path. This both leaves the core security property of recovery codes untested and makes the test provider an unsafe model for real user-storage implementations.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Background reader thread is never joined and can hang the test JVM or let the assertion race

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader thread (new Thread(...).start() at line 139) and only stops it by setting deletedAll in the normal path; there is no try/finally. If anything in the deletion loop throws (e.g. an admin DELETE returns an error) or the test aborts before line 155, deletedAll is never set, so the loop keeps issuing groups() requests forever and the non-daemon thread prevents the test JVM from exiting. In addition, the assertion assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty()) at line 157 executes immediately after deletedAll.set(true) without joining the reader, so a read that is still in flight can record its exception after the assertion runs, allowing a regression to pass unnoticed. The thread should be stopped in a finally block, joined before the assertion, and ideally created as a daemon.

However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the only provider that is actually disambiguated is AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). If two of the real providers land on the classpath together (e.g. a FIPS deployment that also has the default provider), selection among the equal-order providers falls back to the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is not guaranteed stable across filesystems/containers. The result is that a non-FIPS provider can be chosen silently in a deployment that previously failed fast at startup, disabling FIPS without any error. FIPS should have a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers (or the removed guard should be retained for genuinely conflicting providers).

ECDSA round-trip test uses one default-curve key and never verifies the signature

false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each work queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never blocks; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` only records a gauge. If a group's single worker falls behind (e.g. one slow subscription), its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps polling and advancing/committing offsets, consuming memory and risking OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is therefore false. Use a bounded queue (maxsize) and either block in submit() or stop polling when queues are full.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items instead of draining

OrderedQueueWorker.run() tests `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `queue.get()`. In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 231) every worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True, and only afterwards is `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` called. Because the loop exits as soon as the flag is set, a worker processes at most the one item it had already fetched and then drops everything still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain semantics never take effect. In-flight results are silently discarded on a graceful shutdown. The loop should keep calling `get()` and break only when it raises `queue.ShutDown`.

Failed results are still committed and lost (no retry/DLQ)

Offset completion happens in a `finally` block, so `complete_offset()` runs even when `result_processor` raises, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` already swallows all exceptions internally. Combined with the offset tracker, a message whose processing permanently fails is still considered done, committed, and never retried or routed to a DLQ — it is silently lost, contradicting the class docstring's 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Similarly, submit() (line 317) catches exceptions from decoding/grouping and marks the offset complete, dropping those messages. Errors must leave the offset outstanding (or send to DLQ) rather than be committed.

Commit thread stopped before queue drain, leaving work uncommitted

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(). Items still drained by the workers after that point complete their offsets but the commit thread is already dead, so those offsets are never committed and the results are reprocessed on restart (duplicates). terminate() also calls the graceful queue_pool.shutdown() rather than abandoning pending work. The queue should be drained/shut down before the commit thread stops, and terminate/close should have distinct semantics (drop vs flush).

join() ignores its timeout and can block for ~100s

join(timeout) discards the argument and delegates to close(), which calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() joins each worker sequentially with a hard-coded `timeout=5.0`; with the default 20 queues that is up to ~100 seconds of blocking in the worst case, far beyond arroyo's expected join timeout and potentially past the broker's max.poll.interval.ms during shutdown/rebalance. Respect the passed timeout and join workers against a shared deadline.

arroyo Commit invoked from a background thread

The commit function passed into create_with_partitions (arroyo's `Commit`) is called every second from a dedicated `commit_thread`, i.e. concurrently with the consumer's poll loop and rebalance handling, whereas every other mode commits from the strategy's processing thread. arroyo's Commit is not designed for cross-thread invocation; if it is not fully thread-safe this can corrupt or lose committed offsets. Either serialize commit calls onto the strategy thread (a lock coordinated with poll/join) or confirm arroyo's Commit is safe to call from another thread.

Error-handling test asserts behavior the implementation cannot produce

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling patches ResultProcessor.__call__ to raise for the first message and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a failed message blocks the commit. But the worker calls complete_offset() in a `finally` even when result_processor raises, so both offsets 100 and 101 are marked complete and are committed; the assertion will fail. Either the exception handling must leave failed offsets outstanding, or the test's expectation is wrong and must be corrected to match the current commit-on-error behavior.

test_stats_reporting is racy against active workers

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a pool with 3 already-running worker threads and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. The workers can consume all items before get_stats() executes, making total_items 0 and flaking the test. Make it deterministic by asserting on a state that cannot race with consumption (e.g. pause/block the workers, or check committed counts rather than instantaneous queue depth).

For traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 the walk stops before reaching the true segment key, so the span is attached to an intermediate key and the segment can be flushed split/duplicated rather than merged into its root. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

The denial key concatenates user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with literal "_" separators. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores and resource name/folder are caller-controlled, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. A denial cached for one resource would then deny an unrelated resource. false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer checks collide

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, subject UID, action, resource name, and folder, but not the identity type. Anonymous and renderer subjects both resolve to user UID "0" (for example anonymous:0 and render:0), and users and service accounts can also share a UID. A denial written for one principal is therefore returned for another principal on the same action/resource/folder. Concretely, an anonymous Check for dashboards:read/dash1 stores key org-12.perm_0_dashboards:read_dash1_, and a later renderer Check for the same dashboard hits that key and is denied without consulting renderer permissions, breaking rendering. Include the identity type (or full subject type) in the denial key.

Every distinct denied resource name causes a fresh permission DB query

When cached identity permissions exist but do not allow the requested resource, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and queries the permission store. The denial cache only remembers the exact (action, name, parent) tuple, so callers can send checks for arbitrary distinct dashboard/folder UIDs (for example anonymous probes of /api/dashboards/uid/<random>) and force one permission DB query per UID. Previously these cache-hit checks were served without touching the DB. This is a DB-load/DoS regression; consider coalescing or marking a user/action as freshly queried rather than falling back per resource name.

Tests seed the denial cache manually and never verify Check populates it

The new denial-cache test manually calls permDenialCache.Set before invoking Check. There is no test that performs a Check returning false from the permission store and then asserts the denial is written, nor a test that a denial for one identity type does not affect another identity type. As a result, a regression where Check never writes denials, writes them under a mismatched key, or collides anonymous and renderer entries would pass the current test suite.

The newly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` is never used, so all API calls use the old (likely expired) token. The handler never inspects `req.method`, so any verb (GET/PUT/DELETE/...) is accepted as long as the header matches, and `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throwing on an invalid payload surfaces as a 500 instead of a 400. false_positives.candidate:
Uses prisma without importing it

The new token-refresh block in getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update({...})` but the module never imports `prisma` (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, getLocation, WEBAPP_URL, HttpError, logger, calendar types, CredentialPayload, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse). This will fail type-check and throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime whenever a Salesforce credential is used, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

Credential-sync request is sent with no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT includes only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` and no shared secret/authorization, so the self-hoster cannot verify the request actually came from the configured Cal.com instance. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can request credential refreshes for arbitrary user ids/app slugs. It should send an authenticated header derived from a shared secret (analogous to the webhook secret).

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality

`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` compares the shared secret with `!==`, leaking timing information that can be exploited to recover the secret over many requests. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on Buffers of equal length).

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. Past-due cancelled reminders are deleted before they are cancelled
