A reminder cancelled shortly before it is due can therefore be deleted by this deleteMany without ever receiving a SendGrid cancel call. The same cleanup drops cancellations whose SendGrid request failed on a previous run. With a 15-minute cron interval, cancelling a reminder minutes before send can still result in the email being sent. Reschedule still uses direct SendGrid cancellation and bypasses the new cancelled flag

When rescheduling, old email reminders are cancelled with immediateDelete=true. That performs a direct SendGrid scheduled_sends cancel instead of setting cancelled for the cron path. This is the same flow that can hit SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation limit; when the request fails the helper only logs, no cancelled state is persisted, and the old reminder can still be sent after the booking was rescheduled. Normal reschedules should use the deferred cancelled flag, with immediate cancellation only when the send is imminent.

Calendar update uses actor credentials instead of booking owner credentials

The handler fetches booking.user with destinationCalendar and credentials, but then builds EventManager from ctx.user and calls getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). Two concurrent logins with the same backup code can both read the original array and both succeed, violating single-use. Two concurrent logins with different codes can each null a different index, and the last write wins, resurrecting the other already-used code. Use a DB transaction/conditional update or a row per code so consumption is atomic.

The added e2e coverage only verifies that the backup-code screen appears and that download/copy/close controls work. Video references lose credentialId

`referencesToCreate` now sets `credentialId` only for calendar results (`isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`). With this change new video references have no `credentialId`, so deletion paths such as `handleCancelBooking` skip `deleteMeeting` and leave orphaned video meetings.

Location updates create references without externalCalendarId or credentialId

`updateLocation` now builds `referencesToCreate` using `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never returns either field. As a result, after editing a location the newly created booking references omit `externalCalendarId` and `credentialId`, breaking future calendar updates/deletes and forcing legacy fallback behavior. The reference data must be taken from the update result/credential or from the event destination calendar.

Collective team destination calendars dropped when organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. In that case `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op, so destination calendars collected from the other collective hosts are discarded. This means an organizer without a connected calendar prevents other hosts from receiving calendar invites, which is one of the cases this PR is meant to fix. Initialize the array and push unconditionally when team destinations exist.

Lark creates all events in the first host's destination calendar

`createEvent` takes the first destination calendar from the array and ignores which credential called it. With multiple collective hosts, the second host's Lark credential will try to create the event in the first host's calendar id, so the event either fails or lands in the wrong calendar and the second host does not receive the expected invite. The service needs to select the destination corresponding to the credential used.

CalDAV/BaseCalendar silently skips additional hosts

`createEvent` filters available calendars down to the first destination calendar's `externalId`. When EventManager calls this service for the second host's destination, that externalId belongs to the first host's calendar and does not match any calendar for the second credential, so the filter returns an empty list and no event is created. Because empty responses are treated as success, the missing host event is silent. The filter should target the destination for the current credential rather than always the first array element.

The recurring cancellation branch still uses `updatedBooking.references.find(...)` and deletes only the first `_calendar` reference for each booking. With multi-host bookings there are now multiple calendar references, so only one host's recurring events are cancelled while the others remain on calendars. Recurring cancellation API deletes are pushed after Promise.all

After adding `await getCalendar(credential)`, the callback yields before pushing into `apiDeletes`; the later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` therefore sees an empty `apiDeletes` and returns without waiting for those calendar deletions. Recurring calendar events may never be cancelled before the handler finishes. Collect promises with `await Promise.all(...)` or use a `for...of` loop.

Reschedule calendar/video deletion races because async forEach is unawaited

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` is not awaited. The newly added `await getCalendar(...)` yields before `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` is even called, so `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and the function return happen while the original calendar/video event may still be present. Any rejection from `getCalendar` or the delete calls is also an unhandled rejection instead of being caught by the surrounding `try/catch`. Use `for...of` or `await Promise.all(...)`.

Reschedule cleanup starts after the response because async forEach is unawaited

The authenticator now resolves the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which returns the federated (user-storage) credential first when before it only looked at Keycloak's local store. When allCodesUsed() is true the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). In addition, models built from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (the shape the user-storage path produces) do not carry the original stored id, so getId() can be null and passing null into the credential store (JPA EntityManager.find) throws IllegalArgumentException. The local branch instead uses credentialModel, which contains only the hashed codes and per-code used flags (see RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.createFromValues). The new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin does only one login with the first code, so it does not cover the single-use guarantee or the 'all codes used -> re-configure' path. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common, and order() is added as an abstract method rather than a default method. Every existing implementation (including third-party providers and the keycloak-client code the PR description says will be synced later) must now add this method; old implementations that do not will fail to compile / fail at link time. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve compatibility while still letting providers opt into precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider requires existing implementations to implement it. The candidate also proposes a default method to preserve compatibility.

false_positives.candidate:
Multi-provider selection is nondeterministic and removes fail-fast FIPS guard

This change removes the previous guard that threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found, and instead silently picks the highest-order provider. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the only provider that is actually disambiguated is AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). If two of the real providers land on the classpath together (e.g. a FIPS deployment that also has the default provider), selection among the equal-order providers falls back to the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is not guaranteed stable across filesystems/containers. The result is that a non-FIPS provider can be chosen silently in a deployment that previously failed fast at startup, disabling FIPS without any error. FIPS should have a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers (or the removed guard should be retained for genuinely conflicting providers).

The test generates a single `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, normally P-256) and reuses it for ES256/384/512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is idempotent; it never verifies the produced signature with the public key and never exercises the actual 521-bit curve. Because the padding to `signLength` is symmetric, a wrong per-curve length/endianness/truncation would still round-trip and the test would pass. Generating a key per algorithm's curve and asserting Signature.verify would actually validate curve-specific behavior.

New provider-ordering selection logic is not covered by tests

detectProvider now sorts multiple providers by order() and ignores the lower-ordered ones, but there is no test that loads multiple CryptoProviders and asserts the highest-order one is selected (or that ties behave sanely). Given this ordering is the central mechanism of the PR, a test using a custom ServiceLoader/classloader with two known-order providers would guard the selection logic against regressions and would have surfaced the equal-order ambiguity noted for the real providers.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each work queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never blocks; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` only records a gauge. If a group's single worker falls behind (e.g. one slow subscription), its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps polling and advancing/committing offsets, consuming memory and risking OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is therefore false. Use a bounded queue (maxsize) and either block in submit() or stop polling when queues are full.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items instead of draining

OrderedQueueWorker.run() tests `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `queue.get()`. In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 231) every worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True, and only afterwards is `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` called. Because the loop exits as soon as the flag is set, a worker processes at most the one item it had already fetched and then drops everything still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain semantics never take effect. In-flight results are silently discarded on a graceful shutdown. The loop should keep calling `get()` and break only when it raises `queue.ShutDown`.

Failed results are still committed and lost (no retry/DLQ)

Offset completion happens in a `finally` block, so `complete_offset()` runs even when `result_processor` raises, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` already swallows all exceptions internally. Combined with the offset tracker, a message whose processing permanently fails is still considered done, committed, and never retried or routed to a DLQ — it is silently lost, contradicting the class docstring's 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Similarly, submit() (line 317) catches exceptions from decoding/grouping and marks the offset complete, dropping those messages. Errors must leave the offset outstanding (or send to DLQ) rather than be committed.

Commit thread stopped before queue drain, leaving work uncommitted

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(). Items still drained by the workers after that point complete their offsets but the commit thread is already dead, so those offsets are never committed and the results are reprocessed on restart (duplicates). terminate() also calls the graceful queue_pool.shutdown() rather than abandoning pending work. The queue should be drained/shut down before the commit thread stops, and terminate/close should have distinct semantics (drop vs flush).

join() ignores its timeout and can block for ~100s

join(timeout) discards the argument and delegates to close(), which calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() joins each worker sequentially with a hard-coded `timeout=5.0`; with the default 20 queues that is up to ~100 seconds of blocking in the worst case, far beyond arroyo's expected join timeout and potentially past the broker's max.poll.interval.ms during shutdown/rebalance. The commit function passed into create_with_partitions (arroyo's `Commit`) is called every second from a dedicated `commit_thread`, i.e. concurrently with the consumer's poll loop and rebalance handling, whereas every other mode commits from the strategy's processing thread. arroyo's Commit is not designed for cross-thread invocation; if it is not fully thread-safe this can corrupt or lose committed offsets. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

The denial key concatenates user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with literal "_" separators. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores and resource name/folder are caller-controlled, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. A denial cached for one resource would then deny an unrelated resource. Use length-prefixed or escaped components, or hash a structured key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited denial cache keys that can collide when components contain underscores, causing incorrect cache hits and permission denials. The candidate describes the same underlying issue and provides a concrete collision example.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer checks collide

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, subject UID, action, resource name, and folder, but not the identity type. Anonymous and renderer subjects both resolve to user UID "0" (for example anonymous:0 and render:0), and users and service accounts can also share a UID. A denial written for one principal is therefore returned for another principal on the same action/resource/folder. Concretely, an anonymous Check for dashboards:read/dash1 stores key org-12.perm_0_dashboards:read_dash1_, and a later renderer Check for the same dashboard hits that key and is denied without consulting renderer permissions, breaking rendering. Include the identity type (or full subject type) in the denial key.

When cached identity permissions exist but do not allow the requested resource, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and queries the permission store. The denial cache only remembers the exact (action, name, parent) tuple, so callers can send checks for arbitrary distinct dashboard/folder UIDs (for example anonymous probes of /api/dashboards/uid/<random>) and force one permission DB query per UID. Previously these cache-hit checks were served without touching the DB. This is a DB-load/DoS regression; consider coalescing or marking a user/action as freshly queried rather than falling back per resource name.

Tests seed the denial cache manually and never verify Check populates it

The new denial-cache test manually calls permDenialCache.Set before invoking Check. There is no test that performs a Check returning false from the permission store and then asserts the denial is written, nor a test that a denial for one identity type does not affect another identity type. As a result, a regression where Check never writes denials, writes them under a mismatched key, or collides anonymous and renderer entries would pass the current test suite.

A unified-storage create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 45), and a unified-storage update failure is also recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 129), even though no legacy call has happened. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

Mode 3 launches the legacy write in a goroutine using the incoming request context: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. In Go's HTTP server, the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, and these methods return the unified-storage result immediately after starting the goroutine. The legacy `Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` calls (also at lines 110, 135 and 163) therefore commonly run with an already-canceled context, so the shadow write to legacy fails and the safety copy is never made. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving request values) or a fresh context with an explicit timeout.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order

All mode 3 legacy writes are independent goroutines with no per-object serialization. Two sequential updates to the same object can complete their legacy writes in reverse order, leaving legacy with the older state; a delete followed by a re-create can likewise leave the shadow store missing or containing an object after the unified store already reflects the opposite operation. Because the legacy write is meant as a safety copy, this silently makes the two stores diverge. A per-key queue/worker or version/order check is needed if legacy is expected to remain consistent.

Legacy write failures in async mode are never logged

Every async goroutine discards the legacy error and only calls a metrics recording function, e.g. `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. There is no `log.Error`, unlike the previous synchronous implementation. Since these writes are fire-and-forget, operators have no log evidence when the shadow write fails, making the safety mechanism effectively undiagnosable. Log the error (including object identity and method) in each async legacy path.

Create error test configures the wrong store and will hit an unexpected mock call

This change replaces scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) with dark-light-choose using 50% for both branches. It alters the light-theme color to a lighter gray and does not apply the expected complementary $secondary(70%) value in dark themes. The original $primary(30%) value should be preserved.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. This equals the correct ceiling except when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`: e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields `floor(50/50)+1 = 2` pages, and 100 members yields 3 pages, even though there are only 1 and 2 real pages. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` to `totalPages`, the `next` action remains enabled on the real last page; clicking it sets `offset` to `user_count` and loads a completely empty page (the request returns zero members). The formula should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the existing `user_count == 0` guard).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same pagination bug: when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, the next action permits offset == user_count, producing an empty extra page and confusing last-page UX. The candidate additionally explains the off-by-one page-count calculation that enables this behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page now silently truncates to 50 members

The public `members` action used to return every member for non-automatic groups (and up to 200 for automatic groups). It now always applies a `limit` (default 50), but the only consumer that renders the public membership list, `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs`, still iterates `members` with no pagination controls and `Group#findMembers` sends the default limit/offset. As a result any public group with more than 50 members silently shows only the first 50 and offers no way to load the rest. The admin page was given pagination in this PR, but the non-admin group page was not, so this is a regression for large groups. Either the public page needs a pager/see-more, or the old unlimited/200 behavior must be preserved for this endpoint.

Members endpoint response shape changed from array to {members, meta}

`GroupsController#members` previously rendered a bare array of serialized users (`render_serialized members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer`); it now renders `{ members: [...], meta: { total:, limit:, offset: } }`. The route `/groups/:name/members` is a public route, and any client other than the Ember app updated here (mobile apps, plugins, scripts) that expects a top-level array will break. If the shape change is intentional it should at least be called out as an API change, and ideally the old route/format kept or a versioned/new endpoint introduced.

limit/offset on public members endpoint are unbounded and can 500

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are taken directly from request params with no clamping. A caller can pass a very large `limit` to force the server to load and serialize an arbitrarily large result set on this unauthenticated-to-any-user-who-can-see-the-group endpoint, and a negative `offset` produces an `OFFSET -5` query that PostgreSQL rejects (HTTP 500). These should be validated/clamped (e.g. `offset = [params[:offset].to_i, 0].max`, `limit = params[:limit].to_i.clamp(1, 200)`).

New member routes and paginated members endpoint are untested at the routing/HTTP level

The `.add_members`/`.remove_member` specs call controller actions directly with `xhr`, which bypasses routing entirely, so the new routes (`delete/put "members" => groups#add_members/remove_member`) and the `params.require(:group_id)` / `params[:user_id]` contract are never exercised — a verb or `:group_id` vs `:id` mismatch would not be caught. Additionally the new behavior of `GroupsController#members` (the `{members, meta}` shape, `total`/`limit`/`offset` in `meta`, and the removal of the old 200-member automatic-group cap) has no controller spec at all. Add request specs covering the new admin routes and a `GroupsController#members` spec asserting the pagination meta and that limit/offset are honored.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation has write side effects and double-counts blocked matches

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` is a predicate but performs a read-modify-write on `match_count` and saves the record every time it is called. It is called from a model validator, so ordinary `user.valid?` checks mutate the blocklist table. This is especially visible in `UsersController#create`, which calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`: a blocked signup increments `match_count` twice for one attempt. The non-atomic `record.match_count += 1; record.save` also loses increments under concurrent requests. As a result, `match_count`/`last_match_at` are not reliable, and validation requests cause unnecessary writes. Move the statistics update out of the validator or make it an atomic, once-per-actual-attempt operation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: a blocking predicate updates statistics during a read/check operation, introducing unexpected write side effects and concurrency risks. The candidate adds validation and double-counting details without changing the core concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and bypassable

The domain restriction regexp is built without an end anchor. With a whitelist setting of `example.com`, it compiles to `@(example\.com)`, which also matches the prefix of `user@example.com.evil.com`; that address is therefore accepted even though its domain is not whitelisted. Conversely, a blacklist can overblock unrelated hosts. Anchor the match to the actual domain boundary (or parse the domain and compare exact values) instead of using an unanchored substring regexp.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same domain-restriction regex bug: missing full-domain boundary anchoring allows non-whitelisted domains to match. The candidate uses a different bypass example but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case/whitespace sensitive and bypassable

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` compares the raw submitted email with exact string equality. There is no normalization in the new validator or in the User email assignment path, so on a case-sensitive database (Discourse uses PostgreSQL) a blocked address like `spam@example.com` can be submitted as `Spam@example.com` (or with surrounding whitespace) and will not match. The account is then allowed despite the block. Normalize the value before lookup and when storing block records, e.g. strip/downcase consistently and query with the normalized form.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bypass in BlockedEmail.should_block?: case-sensitive email matching allows a differently capitalized version of a blocked address to evade the block. The candidate additionally mentions whitespace, but that does not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Tests stub out the critical block lookup and never cover User validation

Both new validator examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they do not exercise the real database lookup, email normalization, or the `User` validation path. There is also no spec asserting that a `User` with a blocked or mixed-case blocked email is invalid, and no coverage for the whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved from `User` into this validator. These gaps are exactly what would catch the blocklist bypass and the unanchored domain regex. Add model/integration specs using real `BlockedEmail` records and a `User`/`valid?` path.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin does not cover the same legacy engines as flexbox mixin

`@mixin flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box`, but `@mixin align-items()` never emits the matching legacy Mozilla property `-moz-box-align`. In engines that use the old Mozilla box model, the flex container is created but vertical alignment is ignored, so `.d-header .contents` and `.small-action` are not centered as intended. The mixin also emits `-ms-align-items`, which is not a real IE property; the valid property is `-ms-flex-align` (already present). Add `-moz-box-align` or drop the `-moz-box` display, and remove the invalid `-ms-align-items`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies -ms-align-items as an invalid IE property and names -ms-flex-align as the correct replacement, matching the golden issue despite also raising a Mozilla compatibility concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin maps 0-based order values directly to 1-based legacy ordinal groups

The legacy `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` properties are 1-based (default 1), while the modern `order` property is 0-based (default 0). `@mixin order($val)` passes `$val` unchanged to both families. The current callers use `order(2)` and `order(3)`, so relative ordering happens to work, but any future caller using `order(1)` — or relying on parity with the modern default — will get incorrect ordering in legacy engines. The legacy properties should use a 1-based value such as `$val + 1`, or the mixin should document/enforce the difference.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same mismatch: the mixin passes modern order values unchanged to legacy ordinal-group properties, which require values starting at 1. Although the candidate uses a different example, it identifies the same underlying compatibility and layout issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Flexbox on .small-action makes the action button's float ineffective

Adding `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action` makes its children flex items, and `float` is ignored on flex items. The existing `button { float: right; }` at line 309 therefore no longer pushes the button to the right; because `.small-action-desc` has no `flex-grow` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`, the button will sit immediately after the description instead of at the far right. This is a layout regression for small-action rows such as post notices.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name inclusion hook is never called

The method is named include_website_name without the trailing question mark. ActiveModelSerializers looks for include_<attribute>? to decide whether to emit an attribute, so this method is dead code. website_name is therefore emitted for every serialized user, including as null when no website exists, and any inclusion logic placed here is ignored. Rename it to include_website_name? and combine it with the untrusted-field check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing question-mark suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional attribute inclusion. It does not mention the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
New website_name bypasses TL0 website privacy restriction

website_name is added to attributes (line 43) but is missing from untrusted_attributes (lines 105-111). For a TL0 user viewed anonymously, the existing untrusted_attributes :website rule removes the website field, but website_name is still computed from object.user_profile.website and sent to the client. The user profile template renders model.website_name, so the hidden website host and path become visible. The TL0 spec does not catch this because its untrusted_attributes list omits :website_name and its fabricated user has no website. Add :website_name to untrusted_attributes or make the inclusion hook return false when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object), and extend the spec accordingly.

Domain comparison misclassifies unrelated hosts under multi-label public suffixes

The elsif branch treats any two hosts with the same label count greater than two and the same suffix after the first label as the same domain. For example, with instance host foo.co.uk and user website bar.co.uk, both have three labels and suffix co.uk, so the code appends the full path from bar.co.uk even though it is a different registrable domain. The same false positive occurs for foo.github.io and bar.github.io, and similar public suffixes. This defeats the stated same-domain check and can expose a path that would otherwise be hidden. Use a public-suffix-aware registrable-domain comparison or avoid matching multi-label public suffixes this way.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching

The listener validates messages with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`. This accepts any origin that appears as a substring of `discourseUrl`; for example, `http://eviltrout.co` passes when `discourseUrl` is `http://eviltrout.com`. An untrusted window can then send forged `discourse-resize` messages to the embedding page. The origin should be compared exactly against the parsed `discourseUrl` origin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same security flaw: using indexOf substring matching for postMessage origin validation allows malicious origins to bypass the check. The different example domains do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsanitized feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered as cooked HTML

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true` using content taken directly from external RSS/Readability sources. Post#cook returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts, and app/views/embed/best.html.erb renders `raw post.cooked`. A malicious or compromised feed can therefore store `<script>` or event-handler HTML that executes in the Discourse origin (stored XSS). The imported_from footer also interpolates the feed URL into raw HTML without escaping. Imported HTML must be sanitized before storage, or this path must use the normal cooking/sanitization pipeline.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the unescaped feed URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import's generated HTML, matching the golden comment's XSS issue. It does not mention the nil contents NoMethodError, but it identifies the same underlying XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid `end if` makes the best embed view fail to compile

The template closes the header conditional with `<%- end if %>`. There is no condition after the `if`, so Ruby parses this as an incomplete modifier-if and raises a SyntaxError when the template is compiled. Any successful embed request that finds a `topic_id` and renders `best.html.erb` will fail with a 500. It should be `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closure `end if`, which causes a Ruby syntax error during rendering, and recommend replacing it with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed assumes every feed item has `content`

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `scrub` on `i.content` without checking for nil. Many RSS/Atom feeds expose body text only through `description` (or have empty/missing content), in which case `i.content` is nil and the job raises NoMethodError. Since this job sets `retry: false`, such a feed stops importing items. Guard missing content and fall back to `description` or skip the item.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that calling scrub on a nil i.content can crash feed processing when content is missing, and recommend falling back to description.

false_positives.candidate:
Protocol-relative URLs are corrupted during absolutization

The absolutizer treats every href/src beginning with `/` as root-relative. A protocol-relative URL such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png` starts with `/`, so it is rewritten to `http://origin/cdn.example.com/image.png`, breaking links and images in imported feed content. Detect `//` separately and preserve the scheme (or use URI.join).

`open(url)` is used without requiring open-uri

`TopicEmbed.import_remote` calls `open(url)` but this file does not require `open-uri`. Only `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb` requires it, so when the retrieve-topic job or the Disqus task calls `import_remote` first, Ruby's `Kernel#open` treats the URL as a local filename and raises `Errno::ENOENT`. Add `require 'open-uri'` in this file or in every caller before fetching remote content.

Existing migration now drops the top_topics table with `force: true`

This PR changes an already-existing migration from `create_table :top_topics` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. If the migration is ever run against a database where `top_topics` exists but the migration is not recorded (for example after a partially failed migration or a restored schema), Rails will drop the table and all of its rows before recreating it. Migrations should be immutable; use a new migration or guard with `unless table_exists?` instead of adding `force: true`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate self.downsize definition silently replaces the width/height overload

The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby does not support overloading: the second definition replaces the first, so the width/height version is dead code. Any caller using `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, 100, 200)` will now hit the 3-argument method with `dimensions = 100` and `opts = 200`; `optimize` then calls `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer and raises NoMethodError (or, worse, builds `-resize 100` geometry with no aspect handling). The `force_aspect_ratio` path is likewise unreachable through the width/height form. This is an API break for an existing public class method. Use a single signature, or rename the dimensions form (e.g. `downsize_to_dimensions`), or accept both dimensions and options explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same duplicate method definition: the dimensions-based downsize replaces the width/height version, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client validation no longer honors configured max size settings, including for attachments

Replacing `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` raises the client-side limit for every upload type. Only images are downsized server-side; attachments are still rejected by the server against `max_attachment_size_kb`. On a site configured with, say, a 1MB attachment limit, an 8MB PDF now passes `validateUploadedFile`, is uploaded, and only then fails with a server error. The message in `displayErrorForUpload` (line 246) has the same problem: the 413 case hardcodes 10MB and will report the wrong limit whenever the web-server threshold differs. The larger limit should be scoped to images (and ideally still derived from the site settings), leaving attachment limits unchanged.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that hardcoding the upload limit to 10 * 1024 ignores configured per-type site limits, causing client/server limit mismatches, and that the 413 handler likewise reports a hardcoded, potentially incorrect limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and never verifies the target size was reached

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false when the convert/gifsicle step fails, but the loop does not check the return value and never re-checks that the file shrank: it just calls downsize up to five times on the same path and then proceeds to `Upload.create_for` with whatever is on disk. If the image format has no extension on the tempfile path, if ImageMagick cannot parse `80%>` geometry, or if five 80% reductions simply cannot get under `max_image_size_kb`, the loop burns five CPU-heavy conversions and the oversized (or corrupted/truncated, since convert reads and writes the same file) image is uploaded and stored anyway, contrary to the configured limit. Additionally, because `from == to`, a failed convert can leave the tempfile truncated and that corrupt file is still uploaded. Break out on failure and, after the loop, reject the upload with a clear error if `tempfile.size` is still over the limit.

API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB for all upload types

The API download path was previously bounded by `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`; it is now hardcoded to `10.megabytes` regardless of the `type` parameter. This means non-image attachments (e.g. `type=attachment`) supplied via `url` can now make the server download up to 10MB even on sites configured with a much smaller limit, and each such upload may additionally trigger five downsize conversions. The enlarged download bound should be applied only when the target is an image (and arguably should still be a configurable/site-derived limit), not to every API upload.

No tests cover the new automatic-downsize behavior

The PR adds a new synchronous downsize loop plus a new `OptimizedImage.downsize` signature/overload, but no specs are included. There are no tests for: reaching the target size after N reductions, the loop giving up after 5 attempts, conversion failure (return false) being surfaced, the API-URL path, or animated GIFs via `downsize_instructions_animated`. The zero-arity/argument ambiguity between the two `downsize` definitions would also be caught by a simple unit test and currently is not.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe assumes a TopicUser row exists and can raise NoMethodError

The action does TopicUser.find_by(...) and immediately reads tu.notification_level. For any logged-in user who has no topic_users row for that topic, tu is nil and the request raises NoMethodError, returning a 500. Email recipients usually have a row because send_notification_email calls TopicUser.change, but the route is accessible to any logged-in user, e.g. via a forwarded email or manual URL. Using TopicUser.change would upsert the row; it would also update notifications_changed_at/reason and publish the MessageBus notification_level_change event that direct save! currently bypasses.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and accessing its notification_level raises an exception. The candidate's additional details do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Global unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url for every email

The new unsubscribe_link string interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}. Email::MessageBuilder renders this key whenever add_unsubscribe_link is true, but it does not provide a default unsubscribe_url. Any mailer or plugin that passes add_unsubscribe_link: true without also passing unsubscribe_url will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument while building the email, so the email is not sent. This PR only updates the notification mailer and one spec, so the contract break is easy to miss.

State-changing unsubscribe endpoint is a GET with no CSRF protection

GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe changes the current user's notification_level using only the session cookie. A malicious page can embed this URL as an image or link and, for a logged-in user who can see the topic, silently downgrade or mute the user's subscription. Email link scanners can trigger the same state change. The link needs an unguessable per-user token or the mutation needs to be a POST protected by CSRF.

New per-topic unsubscribe behavior has no meaningful test coverage

The spec change only adds unsubscribe_url to an existing builder so it no longer exercises the missing-interpolation path. There is no assertion that the new URL appears in the rendered body or HTML, no controller test for creating/muting a TopicUser, no test for the nil-TopicUser case, and no test for Topic#unsubscribe_url. These omissions leave the 500 on missing TopicUser and the global unsubscribe_link interpolation requirement unguarded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId with empty data is a redundant write that may not bump updatedAt

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` intending to refresh `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. Passing an empty `data` object is a no-op for the columns; Prisma's `@updatedAt` is not reliably applied when there are no fields to change, so the intended timestamp refresh likely does not happen. Furthermore, nothing reads `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` for this feature (the PR states the frontend uses `CalendarCache.updatedAt`), so this is an unnecessary extra DB write on the hot cache-population/webhook path for every credential. Remove it (or pass explicit data and surface it in the UI if it is actually needed).

Any accepted booking or calendar busy time during a date override is therefore ignored for fixed hosts and loose hosts, so a host with a date override can be offered/booked while already busy. If another reminder path ever increments retryCount, or a reminder reaches retryCount >= 2 and is then successfully scheduled, this deletes a reminder that still has a live Twilio message scheduled — leaving an orphaned SMS that will still be delivered. The PR changes scheduling semantics (delete after N failures, increment on failure/error) but adds no tests for the new retryCount logic — neither for the delete threshold (`gt: 1`), nor for the increment on the falsy-schedule path, nor for the catch path. `buildFilterConditions` (line 106) and the org/team authorization builders (lines 164-174, 196-207) return fragments such as `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` or `(teamCond) OR (userCond)` without wrapping the whole expression in parentheses when there is a single element (or when the OR is the resulting top-level expression). `getBaseConditions` currently wraps these as `(${auth}) AND (${filter})`, so it is safe today, but these methods are public (`getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`). false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each work queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never blocks; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` only records a gauge. If a group's single worker falls behind (e.g. one slow subscription), its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps polling and advancing/committing offsets, consuming memory and risking OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is therefore false. Use a bounded queue (maxsize) and either block in submit() or stop polling when queues are full.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items instead of draining

OrderedQueueWorker.run() tests `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `queue.get()`. In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 231) every worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True, and only afterwards is `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` called. Because the loop exits as soon as the flag is set, a worker processes at most the one item it had already fetched and then drops everything still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain semantics never take effect. In-flight results are silently discarded on a graceful shutdown. The loop should keep calling `get()` and break only when it raises `queue.ShutDown`.

Failed results are still committed and lost (no retry/DLQ)

Offset completion happens in a `finally` block, so `complete_offset()` runs even when `result_processor` raises, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` already swallows all exceptions internally. Combined with the offset tracker, a message whose processing permanently fails is still considered done, committed, and never retried or routed to a DLQ — it is silently lost, contradicting the class docstring's 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Similarly, submit() (line 317) catches exceptions from decoding/grouping and marks the offset complete, dropping those messages. Errors must leave the offset outstanding (or send to DLQ) rather than be committed.

Commit thread stopped before queue drain, leaving work uncommitted

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(). Items still drained by the workers after that point complete their offsets but the commit thread is already dead, so those offsets are never committed and the results are reprocessed on restart (duplicates). terminate() also calls the graceful queue_pool.shutdown() rather than abandoning pending work. The queue should be drained/shut down before the commit thread stops, and terminate/close should have distinct semantics (drop vs flush).

join(timeout) discards the argument and delegates to close(), which calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() joins each worker sequentially with a hard-coded `timeout=5.0`; with the default 20 queues that is up to ~100 seconds of blocking in the worst case, far beyond arroyo's expected join timeout and potentially past the broker's max.poll.interval.ms during shutdown/rebalance. The commit function passed into create_with_partitions (arroyo's `Commit`) is called every second from a dedicated `commit_thread`, i.e. concurrently with the consumer's poll loop and rebalance handling, whereas every other mode commits from the strategy's processing thread. arroyo's Commit is not designed for cross-thread invocation; if it is not fully thread-safe this can corrupt or lose committed offsets. Either serialize commit calls onto the strategy thread (a lock coordinated with poll/join) or confirm arroyo's Commit is safe to call from another thread.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental gitlink/submodule added to repository

Substring check misclassifies negated and mixed queries as error-only

`_is_error_focused_query` treats any query containing the literal text `event.type:error` as an error-only query. Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores

The denial key concatenates user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with literal "_" separators. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores and resource name/folder are caller-controlled, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. A denial cached for one resource would then deny an unrelated resource. Use length-prefixed or escaped components, or hash a structured key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw. The denial cache key is built by joining fields with underscores, so different inputs can produce identical keys. That collision can cause incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer checks collide

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, subject UID, action, resource name, and folder, but not the identity type. Anonymous and renderer subjects both resolve to user UID "0" (for example anonymous:0 and render:0), and users and service accounts can also share a UID. A denial written for one principal is therefore returned for another principal on the same action/resource/folder. Concretely, an anonymous Check for dashboards:read/dash1 stores key org-12.perm_0_dashboards:read_dash1_, and a later renderer Check for the same dashboard hits that key and is denied without consulting renderer permissions, breaking rendering. Include the identity type (or full subject type) in the denial key.

Every distinct denied resource name causes a fresh permission DB query

When cached identity permissions exist but do not allow the requested resource, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions and queries the permission store. The denial cache only remembers the exact (action, name, parent) tuple, so callers can send checks for arbitrary distinct dashboard/folder UIDs (for example anonymous probes of /api/dashboards/uid/<random>) and force one permission DB query per UID. Previously these cache-hit checks were served without touching the DB. This is a DB-load/DoS regression; consider coalescing or marking a user/action as freshly queried rather than falling back per resource name.

Tests seed the denial cache manually and never verify Check populates it

The new denial-cache test manually calls permDenialCache.Set before invoking Check. There is no test that performs a Check returning false from the permission store and then asserts the denial is written, nor a test that a denial for one identity type does not affect another identity type. As a result, a regression where Check never writes denials, writes them under a mismatched key, or collides anonymous and renderer entries would pass the current test suite.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

After the fast-path read finds `entryPointAssetsCache == nil` and the goroutine acquires `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`, the cache is never checked again. With two concurrent requests in a non-dev environment, both can observe nil, then serialize on the lock and each call `readWebAssetsFromFile`. The second goroutine performs redundant I/O and, worse, overwrites the cache populated by the first goroutine; if its own read fails, it clobbers a valid cache with nil and reports an error. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` while holding the write lock and return the cached value if it has been populated by another goroutine.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: the double-checked locking in GetWebAssets never re-checks the cache after acquiring the write lock, so goroutines that were waiting on the lock repopulate a cache another goroutine already filled.

This PR specifically fixes a data race, but no test exercises concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`. Without a test that starts multiple goroutines against an uninitialized cache and runs under `-race`, a future regression could reintroduce the race or the missing double-check behavior without being detected.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Unless a tenfold increase in global cleanup frequency is intended and coordinated, this change should be reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same change: the cleanup ticker going from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Both say this raises database load and contention. The candidate adds more detail about long-running cleanups overlapping, but the underlying concern is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
New SQLite batch-size test does not actually exceed SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER

The new test case creates 40,003 annotations, but cleanup is run per annotation type and each type has only about 13,334 rows. Therefore no DELETE statement ever contains more than about 13,334 IDs, which is below SQLite >=3.32's 32,766 parameter limit. The test would still pass if the large-batch/inlining fallback were removed, so it does not verify the boundary it claims to cover. It needs more than 32,766 annotations of a single type (or an equivalent setup producing a single batch above the limit).

SQLite large-batch ID list is built in quadratic time

In the SQLite fallback, the ID list is materialized with repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. This makes construction O(n^2) in the number of IDs; a batch in the tens of thousands can copy gigabytes and create GC pressure during cleanup. Use `strings.Builder`, a byte slice, or `strings.Join` to build the list in linear time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 records several operations under the wrong metric or label

The metrics in this file are mis-attributed. A unified-storage create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 45), and a unified-storage update failure is also recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 129), even though no legacy call has happened. Delete success passes the object `name` as the `kind` argument to `recordStorageDuration` (line 106), which both mislabels the series and creates unbounded `kind` label cardinality. DeleteCollection's async legacy call records `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration` (line 166). These produce incorrect dashboards/alerts and misleading legacy vs. storage latency/error rates.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that Delete success passes the object name as the kind argument to recordStorageDuration, which is the same issue as the golden comment's point about using name instead of options.Kind.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

Mode 3 launches the legacy write in a goroutine using the incoming request context: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. In Go's HTTP server, the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, and these methods return the unified-storage result immediately after starting the goroutine. The legacy `Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` calls (also at lines 110, 135 and 163) therefore commonly run with an already-canceled context, so the shadow write to legacy fails and the safety copy is never made. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving request values) or a fresh context with an explicit timeout.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order

All mode 3 legacy writes are independent goroutines with no per-object serialization. Two sequential updates to the same object can complete their legacy writes in reverse order, leaving legacy with the older state; a delete followed by a re-create can likewise leave the shadow store missing or containing an object after the unified store already reflects the opposite operation. Because the legacy write is meant as a safety copy, this silently makes the two stores diverge. A per-key queue/worker or version/order check is needed if legacy is expected to remain consistent.

Legacy write failures in async mode are never logged

Every async goroutine discards the legacy error and only calls a metrics recording function, e.g. `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. There is no `log.Error`, unlike the previous synchronous implementation. Since these writes are fire-and-forget, operators have no log evidence when the shadow write fails, making the safety mechanism effectively undiagnosable. Log the error (including object identity and method) in each async legacy path.

Create error test configures the wrong store and will hit an unexpected mock call

The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets `setupLegacyFn` to return an error and never sets a `Storage.Create` expectation. Mode 3's `Create` calls `Storage.Create` first, so this test invokes the storage mock without an expectation and fails with a testify panic rather than exercising a unified-storage failure. Configure `setupStorageFn` for the error and, if the legacy path is to be covered, set the legacy expectation separately.

Delete/DeleteCollection success tests do not account for the async legacy mock call

The success cases for `TestMode3_Delete` and `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` only set up the Storage mock. Mode 3 always launches a goroutine that calls `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection`, but there is no legacy expectation and the tests do not wait for the goroutine. With testify's bare `mock.Mock`, the unexpected call panics; even if it did not, the test returns before the legacy write happens and never asserts that the shadow delete occurred. Add legacy expectations and a synchronization mechanism (or refactor to inject a synchronous executor) to verify the async write.

Mode 3 integration subtests read legacy before the async shadow write can complete

The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which assumes writes made through the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy `/api/playlists` API (for example the list comparison around lines 516-531 and `getFromBothAPIs` after k8s create/update/delete). Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so the legacy read can race ahead of the shadow write and see stale or missing data. These mode 3 subtests will be flaky/failing even if the implementation is correct; they need to poll/wait for legacy convergence or use a synchronous test mode for immediate-visibility assertions.

Fallback locales are only preloaded inside ApplicationController, so fallbacks fail outside web requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`, so the fallback chain returned by `FallbackLocaleList` (current locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) is only loaded into the `Simple` backend during HTTP requests. Because the default/`:en` files were never loaded, the `Fallbacks` backend's `super(fallback, ...)` lookups find nothing and the fallback silently does not happen. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read/modify/write

The code decrypts the whole backup-code list, mutates one element to null, and writes the whole encrypted list back. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code can both read the original array and both succeed, violating single-use. Two concurrent logins with different codes can each null a different index, and the last write wins, resurrecting the other already-used code. Use a DB transaction/conditional update or a row per code so consumption is atomic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: the non-atomic read/modify/write of backup codes lets concurrent logins with the same code both succeed, breaking one-time use. The candidate adds an extra scenario, but its core issue is identical to the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login can bypass the password when any totpCode is sent

The new branch accepts `credentials.backupCode` as sufficient to validate the second factor, but the password check above only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`. A request with a valid backup code plus any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips password verification and logs in using only the backup code. Since backup codes are often printed or exported, this defeats the password factor. Password verification must also be required when `credentials.backupCode` is present, or the TOTP-only bypass must be scoped to the trusted `totp` flow.

Backup-code recovery is unreachable for `?totp=` logins

When `totpEmail` is present (the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow used after OAuth/SAML sign-in), `footerText` renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only has Cancel. The new Lost access button that sets `twoFactorLostAccess` exists only in `TwoFactorFooter`, so the `BackupCode` form can never be shown. A 2FA-enabled user who reaches login through this path cannot use their backup codes if the authenticator is lost.

onEnable is skipped if the backup-code dialog is dismissed via Escape/outside click

After `handleEnable` succeeds, 2FA is already enabled server-side and the modal switches to DisplayBackupCodes, but `onEnable()` is only called by the Close button at line 269. The `Dialog` still receives the parent's `onOpenChange`, so pressing Escape or clicking outside closes it without notifying the parent or resetting state. The settings page can remain showing 2FA as disabled, and the user may not have saved the codes. Handle `onOpenChange` or call `onEnable` when entering the backup-code step.

Core backup-code login/disable paths are untested

The added e2e coverage only verifies that the backup-code screen appears and that download/copy/close controls work. It never submits a backup code to `next-auth-options` or the disable endpoint, so the new password/backup-code logic (including the password-bypass and single-use behavior above) is not exercised. Add tests for successful backup-code login, rejection/reuse of a consumed code, and disabling 2FA with a backup code.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button makes it unreachable by keyboard for every PasswordField in the app. Keyboard-only users can no longer toggle password visibility; this is an accessibility regression unrelated to the 2FA feature. Remove the tabIndex or provide an accessible alternative.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
